sections.heading: Resting on what cannot be shaken
sections.text: Father, everything around me changes. People change, circumstances change, even the things I lean on can give way. But Christ and his Word do not move. Teach me to stop treating created things as if they can hold the weight of my soul. Settle me on Christ like a stone on a foundation. Keep me close to him, rooted in him, and carried by him.
theological_themes: Christ alone is the unshakable foundation in a changing created world.
Created goods are not ultimate rests for the soul.
Abiding in Christ means dependence, stability, and life from him.

scripture_references.connection: This passage anchors Christian confidence in the unchanging Christ, which directly supports the prayer’s contrast between a shifting created world and the stability found in him.
Jesus describes his people as needing to abide in him because life and fruitfulness come from him, not from independent strength or created supports.

sections.heading: Receiving every mercy through Christ
sections.text: Every mercy I have comes to me through Jesus. He planned it, bought it, promised it, and brings it to me. Father, make his nearness sweet to me. Let me love the Lamb who gave himself for me, not only with correct thoughts, but with a heart warmed by him.
theological_themes: All saving blessing comes through Christ.
Christ is the Lamb whose sacrifice secures mercy for sinners.
True faith involves both truth and holy affection toward Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul gathers every spiritual blessing under God’s saving purpose in Christ, showing that mercy is not detached from Jesus but planned and given in him.
The gift of the Son is the ground of confidence that God will graciously give his people all they need, matching the prayer’s claim that mercies come through Christ.

sections.heading: Owning what my sin really is
sections.text: When I sin against you, I am not just breaking a rule or making a mistake. I am pushing against your will, your love, and the life you give. No person or thing can comfort me when I have turned from you. And my deepest problem is not only one particular wrong thing I have done, but the way my heart keeps drifting from you—loose, distant, and divided when it should be close to you.
theological_themes: Sin is first and most deeply against God.
Specific sins reveal a deeper estrangement and disorder of the heart.
Created comforts cannot heal guilt before God.

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession shows that sin, even when it harms others, is fundamentally an offense against God, which grounds the prayer’s direct honesty before the Father.
Isaiah names sin as a real separation between people and God, illuminating the prayer’s concern with distance, disunion, and estrangement from him.

sections.heading: Holding on to the Mediator
sections.text: But you have given me your Son. Jesus stands between you and my guilty soul—not to keep me away from you, but to bring me back to you. He is the only one who can reach both sides of the pit I have fallen into. He alone spans the gap sin opened. He alone satisfies your justice and brings me home. Help me lay hold of him by faith today, not as an idea far away, but as my living Mediator, worthy of my whole trust because of his love.
theological_themes: Jesus Christ is the only Mediator between God and sinners.
Christ’s atoning work satisfies divine justice and reconciles sinners to God.
Faith lays hold of Christ personally, not merely as a doctrine but as the living Savior.

scripture_references.connection: This text explicitly presents Christ as the one Mediator who gives himself as a ransom, directly grounding the prayer’s trust in Jesus as the only bridge between God and sinners.

Peter describes Christ’s suffering for sins as the righteous for the unrighteous in order to bring us to God, which closely matches the prayer’s movement from guilt and distance to reconciliation through Christ.

sections.heading: Meeting Christ in his Word
sections.text: Father, teach me to know that Jesus is dear to me by how I receive his Word. He comes near to me there. By his Word he gives himself to me, and by faith I receive him. If I resist your Word, I am resisting my Lord at the very place where he is speaking to me. If I welcome your Word, I am welcoming him as he draws near.
theological_themes: Christ makes himself known through his Word.
Faith receives Christ as he is offered and revealed in the Word.
To reject God’s Word is to reject the Lord who speaks through it.

scripture_references.connection: John identifies Christ as the eternal Word made flesh, giving biblical depth to the prayer’s focus on Christ the Word and the way God reveals himself in him.
Jesus connects love for him with keeping his word and says that rejecting his words is rejecting the Father who sent him, supporting the prayer’s link between receiving the Word and receiving Christ.
Paul teaches that faith comes through hearing the word of Christ, which fits the prayer’s emphasis on the Word as the means by which faith lays hold of Christ.

sections.heading: Being shaped into the likeness of Jesus
sections.text: You hold every human heart in your hand, and you hold mine too. Shape my heart by your Word. Make me more like your Son in what I love, what I hate, what I trust, and how I live. Then Christ the Word, and the written Word that reveals him, will be my strength when I am weak and my comfort when I am troubled.
theological_themes: God sovereignly forms the believer’s heart.
The Word sanctifies and shapes believers into Christ’s likeness.
Christ and his Word strengthen and comfort God’s people.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus prays that the Father would sanctify his people in the truth and identifies God’s Word as that truth, grounding the request to be shaped by the Word.
Paul presents conformity to the image of the Son as God’s purpose for his people, which supports the prayer’s desire for the heart to be formed after Christ.
The psalmist asks to be strengthened according to God’s word, making it an apt support for the prayer’s closing confidence that Christ’s Word becomes strength and comfort.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about Christ and his Word can sound like it collapses Christ, the eternal Word, into Scripture. This adaptation keeps both emphases while distinguishing Christ the living Word from the written Word that reveals him.

The statement that all mercies are 'designed, purchased, promised, effected' through Christ reflects a robust Reformed view of providence and redemption. The adaptation preserves the claim in broadly biblical terms without trying to resolve every theological question about common grace and saving mercy.
significant_interpretive_choices: The image of the mediator as a 'middle-man' in a pit was rendered as Christ reaching both sides of the pit and spanning the gap opened by sin, to keep the concrete image while making it intelligible today.
The phrase 'loose spirit towards thee' was interpreted as a heart that is drifting, divided, and not firmly attached to God, rather than as emotional instability in a modern psychological sense.

The line 'I am one with him by the Word on his part, and by faith on mine' was expressed as Christ giving himself through the Word and the believer receiving him by faith, preserving the Word-and-faith dynamic without suggesting that faith is a meritorious contribution.
